<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Mayank Mittal, Fan Yang, Alexander Hansson, 
<br class="ltx_break">Amir Bar, Cesar Cadena, and Marco Hutter
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span> Robotic Systems Lab (RSL), ETH Zurich, Switzerland
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span> Stanford University, Stanford, USA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span> UC Berkeley, Berkeley, USA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span> NVIDIA, Zurich, Switzerland
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Depth sensors are widely deployed across robotic platforms, and advances in fast, high-fidelity depth simulation have enabled robotic policies trained on depth observations to achieve robust sim-to-real transfer for a wide range of tasks. Despite this, representation learning for depth modality remains underexplored compared to RGB, where large-scale foundation models now define the state of the art. To address this gap, we present DeFM, a self-supervised foundation model trained entirely on depth images for robotic applications. Using a DINO-style self-distillation objective on a curated dataset of 60M depth images, DeFM learns geometric and semantic representations that generalize to diverse environments, tasks, and sensors. To retain metric awareness across multiple scales, we introduce a novel input normalization strategy. We further distill DeFM into compact models suitable for resource-constrained robotic systems. When evaluated on depth-based classification, segmentation, navigation, locomotion, and manipulation benchmarks, DeFM achieves state-of-the-art performance and demonstrates strong generalization from simulation to real-world environments. We release all our pretrained models, which can be adopted off-the-shelf for depth-based robotic learning without task-specific fine-tuning. <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Webpage: <span class="ltx_ref ltx_nolink ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_ref_self">https://de-fm.github.io/</span></span></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Index Terms: </h6>Foundation Models, Representation Learning, Robotics, Reinforcement Learning, Navigation, Manipulation

</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span></h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Foundation models pretrained on large-scale RGB datasets have transformed visual representation learning in recent years. Methods such as DINO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, and CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> have become the de facto standard for vision tasks, demonstrating remarkable zero-shot transfer to classification, detection, segmentation, and retrieval. Their success has extended into robotics, where pretrained RGB encoders serve as the backbone for various tasks such as manipulation, navigation, and scene understanding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. Specialized  <a href="#id20"><span href="#id20" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">VFM</span></a> (<a href="#id20"><abbr href="#id20" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">VFM</abbr></a>) tailored to robotics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>, further highlights the central role of large-scale self-supervised representation learning in enabling embodied agents.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, RGB-only observations are challenging to use for robotics, particularly in the context of sim-to-real transfer, which is a central paradigm in robot learning.
This difficulty arises because simulated RGB rarely captures real-world visual complexity. In contrast, depth is invariant to lighting, texture, and color variation, establishing it as highly effective for generalization and sim-to-real transfer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. Depth sensors are now ubiquitous across robotic platforms, including manipulators, mobile robots, drones, and AR/VR devices, and have been leveraged for locomotion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, navigation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, and manipulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. This widespread adoption highlights depth as an important modality for scalable representation learning in robotics, especially when robustness and generalization are required.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the benefits of depth modality, surprisingly, today, no pretrained general-purpose depth encoders exist. Current approaches either re-purpose RGB-pretrained encoders for depth by applying colormaps or channel stacking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, which introduces distribution mismatch and degrades geometric fidelity, or they train task-specific depth encoders from scratch <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, leading to poor generalization across tasks, environments, and sensors. Self-supervised learning on depth remains underexplored, despite the fact that depth inherently captures critical cues for robotics, including metric geometry (e.g., object size and distance), free space (e.g., occupancy), and physical affordances, which are the action possibilities an object offers a robot, such as grasping. Given the availability and advantages of depth data, we raise the natural question:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Can we build a universal pretrained depth encoder for robotics ?</em></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">The simple answer is yes. In this work, we present DeFM, a dedicated self-supervised foundation model trained exclusively on depth images that demonstrates highly effective, transferable features for embodied agents.
As a first qualitative result, we show that the feature space learned by DeFM is fundamentally sound: embeddings from the depth encoder reveal emergent semantic clustering when visualized via PCA (Fig. <a href="#S5.F5" title="Fig. 5 ‣ V-A Foundational Depth Image Understanding ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), mirroring the structure observed in effective RGB representations. This confirms that even without texture or color, semantic information can be extracted from depth, highlighting that the model captures information beyond pure geometry.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">DeFM leverages a DINO-style self-distillation objective applied to our curated dataset. We discuss key design choices for depth pretraining, including the importance of preserving metric depth, input normalization, and dataset mixtures for cross-domain generalization.
To enable practical use in resource-constrained robotics settings, we distill our largest DeFM (ViT-L) into lightweight models ranging from <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> parameters, spanning both convolutional networks (ResNet, EfficientNet, RegNet) and compact transformers (ViT-S).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Most critically, we demonstrate that DeFM can be applied <em id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">frozen</em> across a broad spectrum of robotics tasks. Evaluated on depth-based classification, segmentation, locomotion, navigation, and manipulation, DeFM consistently outperforms RGB-pretrained encoders repurposed for depth (Fig. <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>). This includes task-specific encoder baselines trained from scratch as well as state-of-the-art RGB foundation models adapted to depth. In summary, we make the following key contributions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present DeFM, the first large-scale self-supervised foundation model specifically for depth images with a focus on robotic tasks.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We curate a dataset of <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>60</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> depth images and release distilled models ranging from <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> parameters, covering both CNNs and ViTs, to enable wide adoption in robotics research.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a novel input normalization strategy to retain metric awareness across multiple scales.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">DeFM achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse perception tasks, including classification, segmentation, and various RL-based robotics tasks, including locomotion, navigation, and manipulation, with robust sim-to-real transfer.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Related Work</span></h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS1.4" class="ltx_text">II-A</span> </span><span id="S2.SS1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Vision Foundation Models</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early visual representation learning relied on supervised pretraining on large-scale classification datasets. Convolutional networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite> achieved strong performance when trained on datasets such as Imagenet-21k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>. The introduction of  <a href="#id23"><span href="#id23" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">ViT</span></a> (<a href="#id23"><abbr href="#id23" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">ViT</abbr></a>) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> demonstrated that scaling model capacity and data, e.g., using proprietary datasets such as JFT-300M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, further improved performance across several benchmarks. However, features learned primarily for image classification often transfer sub-optimally to dense prediction tasks like segmentation or geometric prediction without extensive task-specific fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These limitations, along with the limited availability of labeled data, motivated a shift toward  <a href="#id19"><span href="#id19" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">SSL</span></a> (<a href="#id19"><abbr href="#id19" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">SSL</abbr></a>), which leverages the structure of raw data to define supervisory signals without human annotation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>. <a href="#id20"><abbr href="#id20" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">VFM</abbr></a> refer to large, pretrained visual encoders designed to learn general-purpose representations that transfer effectively across a wide range of downstream tasks and domains without any finetuning. <a href="#id19"><abbr href="#id19" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">SSL</abbr></a> has become a dominant pretraining paradigm for these models due to its scalability and domain flexibility. Below, we summarize the common <a href="#id19"><abbr href="#id19" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">SSL</abbr></a> pretraining objectives.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS1.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">II-A</span>1 </span>Contrastive Learning</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Contrastive methods such as SimCLR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>, learn visual representations by maximizing the similarity between different augmented views of the same image. Extending this paradigm, multi-view formulations such as Contrastive Multiview Coding (CMC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> leverage multiple heterogeneous views of an image to strengthen invariance and improve cross-view feature alignment. MoCo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> introduces a momentum-updated encoder and a large, dynamically maintained memory bank, enabling contrastive training with massive negative sets and strong performance at scale.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS1.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">II-A</span>2 </span>Self-Distillation</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Self-distillation methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> use two network branches processing different augmented views of the same image. The student is optimized to predict the representation of a teacher. Collapse is prevented through architectural asymmetry—typically by updating the teacher via a momentum-based running average of the student, allowing stable learning without negative pairs. DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> extends this framework to large-scale curated datasets with improved training recipes and regularization, yielding highly transferable dense features for diverse downstream tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS1.SSS3.4" class="ltx_text">II-A</span>3 </span>Masked Image Modeling (MIM)</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Methods such as MAE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> reconstruct randomly masked regions of an image conditioned on the visible patches, encouraging the encoder to capture global structure while remaining computationally efficient. iBOT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> extends this paradigm by combining MIM with DINO-style self-distillation, jointly predicting patch-level tokens and global representations to produce stronger dense features. Building on this idea, DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> updates the training recipe by separating the MIM and DINO projection heads, assigning training examples to prototypes using Sinkhorn–Knopp algorithm, and scaling both the number of prototypes and the size of the curated training dataset. More recently, in DINOv3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, the authors further scale up the training dataset to an order of magnitude higher (1.7B images) and introduce gram anchoring to prevent degradation of dense feature maps during a long training schedule. I-JEPA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite> adopts a non-generative masked prediction objective that predicts high-level latent representations rather than pixels, leading to semantically rich and stable foundational features. We draw inspiration from these approaches to build a foundational model on depth images.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS1.SSS4.4" class="ltx_text">II-A</span>4 </span>Vision-Language Modeling</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite> and its variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> introduce a powerful form of self-supervision by learning to align visual representations with corresponding natural language captions using a contrastive loss on massive web-scraped datasets. This objective grants the model exceptional zero-shot transfer capabilities and strong semantic grounding, allowing it to solve classification and retrieval tasks using only text prompts. However, while VLMs are semantically rich, their representations are often less spatially and geometrically detailed than those produced by dense visual SSL models like DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond general RGB models, a recent trend is the emergence of specialized geometric foundation models that explicitly unify multiple 3D tasks. Models like DUSt3R <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite> and its successor MASt3R <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite> cast 3D reconstruction as a direct regression problem, predicting unified geometric outputs including dense depth, relative pose, and pointmaps from unconstrained image pairs. Similarly, VGGT (Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite> tackles sequence-based 3D reconstruction by leveraging transformer architectures for robust geometric understanding. Most recently, Depth Anything 3 (DA3) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite> demonstrates that powerful geometric priors can be distilled into a single, simple model by using a plain transformer backbone (e.g., DINO encoder) and a singular depth-ray prediction objective to achieve state-of-the-art performance in multi-view geometry and camera pose estimation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, a complementary trend is Agglomerative Vision Models, such as RADIO (Reduce All Domains Into One) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>, which train a single student model by distilling the knowledge from multiple pre-trained, heterogeneous <a href="#id20"><abbr href="#id20" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">VFM</abbr></a> (e.g., CLIP, DINOv2, SAM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>). This multi-teacher distillation approach efficiently consolidates the diverse strengths, such as zero-shot text grounding and dense correspondence, into a unified encoder, creating a single, versatile backbone for downstream tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS2.4" class="ltx_text">II-B</span> </span><span id="S2.SS2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Visual Representations for Robot Learning</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The features learned by early RGB VFMs are often insufficient for robotics, which requires grounded, action-relevant features emphasizing geometry and physical affordances over general semantics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>. This limitation has driven the development of pretrained visual representations specifically tailored for embodied intelligence.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS2.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">II-B</span>1 </span>Action-Centric Pretraining</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A key approach involves pretraining encoders on large-scale action-centric video datasets to learn representations with temporal and kinematic priors. R3M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> performs pretraining on in-the-wild video (Ego4D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>) using contrastive and video-language objectives. R3M’s frozen encoder improves manipulation success rates by 10-20% over scratch or CLIP baseline models on a suite of tasks. Similarly, VIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite> uses a value-implicit objective, leveraging the relationship between visual observations and expected future rewards to learn representations that inherently capture value and utility for control. More recently MAPLE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite> exploits rich manipulation priors learned from large-scale egocentric videos by predicting fine-grained hand-object contact points and hand poses to enable efficient policy learning for complex downstream tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS2.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">II-B</span>2 </span>Generative and Predictive Modeling</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Another major direction adapts the MIM objective to the robotics domain. MVP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> trains <a href="#id23"><abbr href="#id23" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">ViT</abbr></a> encoders by reconstructing masked patches in robot demonstration videos. This technique was scaled to real-world scenarios <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite> and extended in models like Multi-view Masked World Models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite> to leverage multi-camera views, enabling better 3D consistency. More advanced geometric extensions, such as 3D-MVP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite>, explicitly integrate geometric information from multiple views during pretraining to improve 3D spatial reasoning for manipulation. The emergence of 4D Visual Pre-training (FVP) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite> further highlights the importance of incorporating spatio-temporal dynamics into the pretraining objective.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS2.SSS3.4" class="ltx_text">II-B</span>3 </span>Zero-Shot Transfer of VFMs for Robotics</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With the advancements of VFMs, they are now being increasingly used for various robotic tasks without fine-tuning. For instance, DINOBot <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite> uses DINO features for semantic retrieval and pixel-level alignment to enable one-shot imitation learning, significantly improving data efficiency. Other methods integrate DINOv2 features into voxel representations for bimanual manipulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite> or use them for zero-shot planning within a World Model framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite>. This suggests that the dense, robust feature space learned by DINOv2 is a strong prior for robotics. Some works, such as Theia <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, propose distilling the knowledge from multiple different VFMs into a single, smaller backbone showcasing improvements over a single VFM backbone across diverse robotics tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS3.4" class="ltx_text">II-C</span> </span><span id="S2.SS3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Reinforcement Learning from Depth</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Depth sensing, in contrast to RGB, provides direct access to metric, three-dimensional geometry, which is crucial for grounded robotic interaction and robust sim-to-real transfer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite>. This property has led to extensive research focusing on training end-to-end RL policies directly from depth for various manipulation, locomotion, and navigation tasks.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS3.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">II-C</span>1 </span>Locomotion and Navigation</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In legged and mobile robotics, accurate knowledge of terrain geometry is crucial for robust locomotion and navigation. Earlier works addressed perceptive locomotion by converting depth sensor data into explicit geometric structures, such as height maps or elevation maps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>. While these explicit maps are straightforward to render in simulation, they often suffer from significant noise, require highly accurate odometry, and are challenging to reliably obtain in real-world scenarios due to the limited Field of View (FoV) of ego-centric depth cameras, frequently leading to a sim-to-real gap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>]</cite>. To address these limitations, a major shift involved learning end-to-end policies directly from egocentric depth observations via RL. Agarwal <span id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al</span>.  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite> were among the first ones to demonstrate an end-to-end locomotion system capable of traversing challenging terrains (stairs, curbs, stepping stones) using a quadruped robot equipped with only a single front-facing depth camera. Subsequent methods have built on this foundation, utilizing egocentric depth for more complex behaviors such as parkour <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>, <a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite> and learning local obstacle avoidance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>]</cite>. More recently, this paradigm has been extended to humanoid locomotion, where the robustness requirements are even more stringent. Approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>, <a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>]</cite> train depth-only RL policies and focus on realistic depth synthesis to bridge the sim-to-real gap for complex environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For navigation in diverse, large-scale environments, depth is also a critical input. Platforms like Habitat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite> enable large-scale RL training for tasks such as PointGoal Navigation, where agents frequently use depth or depth-derived features to achieve near-perfect performance in previously unseen environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>. This necessity for robust visual priors also motivates auxiliary pretraining; for instance, in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, the authors introduce a spatially enhanced memory unit and demonstrate improved sim-to-real transfer of the navigation policy by leveraging a frozen Variational Auto Encoder (VAE) pretrained on a large-scale depth dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS3.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">II-C</span>2 </span>Manipulation and Grasping</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Depth perception is a critical modality for manipulation and contact-rich tasks in robotics.
Various approaches use depth images to construct explicit representations such as voxel grids <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite>, point clouds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>]</cite>, or object meshes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">75</a>]</cite>, which are provided to the policy as input.
Although shown effective for manipulation, these methods often struggle with cluttered or dynamic scenes and require careful calibration of perception pipelines. To overcome these limitations, recent research has shifted towards end-to-end policies that directly consume egocentric visual observations.
Zeng <span id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al</span>.  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>]</cite> propose a Q-Learning framework to train dense affordance maps on visual RGB-D observations to clear cluttered scenes. Kalashnikov <span id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al</span>.  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>]</cite> by using continuous Q-learning on large-scale real robot data to train general closed-loop grasping policies in a continuous action space. However, both approaches operate with a simpler, binary action space for a two-fingered gripper.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Due to the high-dimensional control space of dexterous hands, recent works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>, <a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>, <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>, <a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">80</a>]</cite> adopt a teacher-student training paradigm, where a teacher policy receives privileged proprioceptive information and is distilled into a student policy that relies solely on visual observations.
Singh <span id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al</span>.  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite> train a student policy on synthetic stereo RGB images and employ extensive domain randomization and image augmentation to handle visual sim-to-real gaps, which results in long training times. To further address the realization gap between teacher and student policies, their recent work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite> provides the teacher with depth observations alongside privileged proprioceptive inputs. They demonstrate that distilling such a teacher into an RGB-based student results in more robust manipulation policies.
In contrast, Zhang <span id="S2.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">et al</span>.  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> train a teacher policy using the full point cloud of the object and distill it to a student policy that receives only a partial point cloud of the scene obtained from a single-view depth image.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S2.SS3.SSS3.4" class="ltx_text">II-C</span>3 </span>The Untapped Potential of Depth Foundation Models</h4>

<div id="S2.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This extensive body of literature confirms two critical facts: 1) Depth is a popular modality for effective sim-to-real and geometric control due to its invariance to light/texture and the ease of high-fidelity simulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">81</a>, <a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">82</a>, <a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">83</a>]</cite>; and 2) geometric and semantic reasoning is crucial for success in core robotics tasks. However, a critical gap remains: nearly all referenced RL and visual control methods relying on depth use custom, task-specific encoders. These encoders are typically trained from scratch alongside the policy, which is inefficient and restricts the learned representation’s generalization to the specific task and environmental domain in which it was trained. This highlights the lack of available depth encoders trained using a large-scale VFM pretraining objective. We argue that the same self-supervised scaling laws that revolutionized RGB vision (Sec. <a href="#S2.SS1" title="II-A Vision Foundation Models ‣ II Related Work ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II-A</span></a>) must be applied to the depth modality. By introducing DeFM, we close this gap by providing the first large-scale depth foundation model for robotics, generating robust, semantic-aware features capable of universal transfer across the diverse locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks reviewed here.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Prelimnaries</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The success of the DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> in learning highly generalizable and robust visual features makes it the ideal foundation for our DeFM. DINOv2 achieves state-of-the-art performance on dense prediction tasks, such as depth estimation and semantic segmentation, even when its weights are frozen. This demonstrates that its self-supervised objective is uniquely effective in capturing the precise spatial and metric information essential for robotics, making it a suitable <a href="#id19"><abbr href="#id19" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">SSL</abbr></a> paradigm for transferring to the depth modality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The core of the DINOv2 approach is a self-distillation objective applied to a <a href="#id23"><abbr href="#id23" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">ViT</abbr></a> architecture, training a student network to match the output distribution of a momentum-updated teacher network. Its self-supervision comprises of two main objectives along with some enhancements, which we discuss below:</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S3.SS0.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">III-</span>1 </span>Image-Level Objective</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.SS0.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>DINO</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the standard DINO cross-entropy loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> between the student’s output probability distribution (<math id="S3.SS0.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>) and the teacher’s target distribution (<math id="S3.SS0.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>). Both distributions are derived from the ViT’s class token (cls) features, extracted from different augmented views of the same image. The student’s parameters are updated via backpropagation, while the teacher’s weights are constructed using an exponential moving average (momentum update) of the student’s past weights.</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}=-\sum p_{t}\log p_{s}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>DINO</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}=-\sum p_{t}\log p_{s}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S3.SS0.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">III-</span>2 </span>Patch-Level Objective</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S3.SS0.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>iBOT</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}</annotation></semantics></math> enhances spatial consistency by adapting the iBOT framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>. This objective applies the cross-entropy loss between the student’s prediction (<math id="S3.SS0.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{si}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{si}</annotation></semantics></math>) for randomly masked input patches and the teacher’s target distribution (<math id="S3.SS0.SSS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{ti}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{ti}</annotation></semantics></math>) derived from the corresponding visible patches in the teacher network. By forcing the student to predict the teacher’s features for masked tokens, this term explicitly promotes the learning of dense spatial correspondences.</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}=-\sum_{i}p_{ti}\log p_{si}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>iBOT</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}=-\sum_{i}p_{ti}\log p_{si}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S3.SS0.SSS3.4" class="ltx_text">III-</span>3 </span>Objective Enhancements</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DINOv2 employs two critical enhancements for stable and effective large-scale training:</p>
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(a)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">KoLeo Regularizer: To prevent the collapse of the feature space and maintain feature diversity, a repulsive term known as the KoLeo regularizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib84" title="" class="ltx_ref">84</a>]</cite> is added to the loss. This term encourages the features to be dispersed across the feature manifold.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(b)</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sinkhorn-Knopp Centering: The teacher outputs are stabilized and normalized using the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm, replacing the previously used softmax-centering step, leading to stability and preventing model collapse.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Depth Foundation Model</span></h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS1.4" class="ltx_text">IV-A</span> </span><span id="S4.SS1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Overview</span></h3>

<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.18923v1/4_1_dino_architecture_nord_v2.png" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/222;" width="429" height="222" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 2: </span>Overview of the self-supervised pretraining of DeFM.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first train our largest model, a ViT-L with <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="307\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>307</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">307\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> parameters, on our curated depth dataset (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2" title="IV-B Dataset ‣ IV Depth Foundation Model ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-B</span></a>). Since it is crucial to learn metric-aware features at diverse scales, we introduce a novel input normalization strategy (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS3" title="IV-C Input Normalization ‣ IV Depth Foundation Model ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-C</span></a>). We then distill the knowledge from DeFM ViT-L into smaller, lightweight architectures (e.g., ViT-S, ResNets) for resource-constrained robotic deployment (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS5" title="IV-E Distillations ‣ IV Depth Foundation Model ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV-E</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our pretraining leverages a DINO-style self-distillation objective adapted for the depth modality, as shown in Fig. <a href="#S4.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ IV-A Overview ‣ IV Depth Foundation Model ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. For a given input depth image <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, we prepare <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> large <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">global crops</span> (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>) and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> smaller <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">local crops</span> (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>) by applying various geometric and photometric augmentations tailored for depth. The <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">global crops</span> are processed by the momentum-updated teacher network (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>) to produce the target distributions <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. The student network (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>) processes the local crops and the partially masked global crops (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{\prime}_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{\prime}_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>). Three primary losses are then applied to align the student’s output with the teacher’s targets:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DINO <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Global Crops</span> Loss (<math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{Global}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>Global</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{Global}}</annotation></semantics></math>): This loss aligns the student’s representation of the partially masked global crops (<math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x^{\prime}_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x^{\prime}_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>) with the teacher’s representation of the unmasked global crops (<math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>). It operates on the <math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{cls}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝚌𝚕𝚜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{cls}</annotation></semantics></math> token features:</p>
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{Global}}=\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{G}\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}(f_{s}(x^{\prime}_{gi}),f_{t}(x_{gj}))" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>Global</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>G</mi></munderover><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></mrow><mi>G</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>DINO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{Global}}=\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{j=1,j\neq i}^{G}\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}(f_{s}(x^{\prime}_{gi}),f_{t}(x_{gj}))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">DINO <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Local Crops</span> Loss (<math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{Local}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>Local</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{Local}}</annotation></semantics></math>): This term aligns the student’s representations of the local crops (<math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>) with the teacher’s representations of the global crops (<math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{g}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{g}</annotation></semantics></math>). This is computed between the <math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{cls}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝚌𝚕𝚜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{cls}</annotation></semantics></math> tokens:</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{Local}}=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}(f_{s}(x_{l}),f_{t}(x_{g}))" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>Local</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>G</mi></munderover><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>DINO</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{Local}}=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}(f_{s}(x_{l}),f_{t}(x_{g}))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">iBOT <span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Patch Loss</span> (<math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>iBOT</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}</annotation></semantics></math>): This loss is essential for learning dense spatial features. It applies the cross-entropy loss between the student’s feature prediction (<math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{si}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{si}</annotation></semantics></math>) for randomly masked input patches and the teacher’s target distribution (<math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{ti}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{ti}</annotation></semantics></math>) derived from the corresponding visible patches in the teacher network:</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}=-\sum_{i\in\text{masked}}p_{ti}\log p_{si}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>iBOT</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mtext>masked</mtext></mrow></msub><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}=-\sum_{i\in\text{masked}}p_{ti}\log p_{si}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The total loss is the weighted sum of these three terms, along with the KoLeo regularizer to prevent model collapse, as detailed in Sec. <a href="#S3" title="III Prelimnaries ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS2.4" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span> </span><span id="S4.SS2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Dataset</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, the development of a strong foundation model necessitates both scale and diversity in pretraining data. For a depth-specific foundation model tailored for robotics, this need is crucial: the encoder must learn robust geometric and semantic priors spanning a wide range of scales and tasks, from centimeter-scale dexterous manipulation to large-scale outdoor navigation and autonomous driving.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this challenge, we curated a dataset totaling <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60.4\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>60.4</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60.4\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> depth images, combining 18 distinct datasets (Tab. <a href="#S4.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ IV-B Dataset ‣ IV Depth Foundation Model ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>). This collection is broadly classified into three types based on the depth image source, ensuring maximal coverage across sensor fidelity and domain:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE): While the RGB domain benefits from curated, large-scale object-centric datasets (e.g., ImageNet-21k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>), no equivalent diverse dataset exists for depth. To ensure DeFM learns strong object-centric priors for various entities—such as cups, fruits, tools, etc, we leverage these RGB datasets by converting them into depth images using an off-the-shelf MDE network <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">85</a>]</cite>. This MDE-derived data significantly contributes to our overall scale and instills generalized object semantics in the encoder.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Synthetic: These datasets provide clean, noise-free metric depth images and offer domain diversity costly to replicate at scale in the real world.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Real: This category provides the noise characteristics inherent in real robotic sensor data. By incorporating diverse real-world sources collected with different depth sensors, the model learns to be robust and invariant to common sensor artifacts, missing data, and noise profiles. Learning these noise-invariant features is critical for effective sim-to-real transfer in robotic deployments.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, the mixture of these sources provides a balance in diversity, scale, and noise fidelity, thereby maximizing the learned representation’s ability to generalize across diverse, unknown robotic environments.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">TABLE I: </span>Overview of depth pretraining dataset collection. MDE denotes monocular depth estimator.</figcaption>

<td id="S4.T1.1.8.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-top:0.5pt;padding-bottom:0.5pt;">5.8</td></tr>
