<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS3.4" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span> </span><span id="S4.SS3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Input Normalization</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A depth foundation model must operate effectively across an exceptionally wide range of depth scales, from millimeter-level precision required in dexterous manipulation to tens or even hundreds of meters in outdoor navigation. Such a model must preserve metric depth while attending to fine-grained details in the scene. In practice, however, near-field depth variations matter disproportionately more for robotic decision-making (e.g., avoiding an obstacle at <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\text{\,}\mathrm{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\text{\,}\mathrm{m}</annotation></semantics></math>) than those in the far-field. This observation motivates the use of logarithmic depth compression, which enhances sensitivity to close-range structure while smoothly compressing large depth values, a strategy widely employed in autonomous driving and depth-estimation systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib101" title="" class="ltx_ref">101</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Rather than choosing a single input normalization strategy, we thus propose a three-channel log-compressed depth representation to capture depth structure across all operational regimes while preserving metric scale. Let</p>
<table id="S4.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log_{p}(D)=\log(1+D)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log_{p}(D)=\log(1+D)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">denote the standard <span id="S4.SS3.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">log1p</span> transform. From the raw metric depth <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct three complementary channels:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S4.I3" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Global Log-Scaled Depth:
This channel normalizes the log-compressed depth using the minimum (<math id="S4.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\min}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\min}</annotation></semantics></math>) and maximum (<math id="S4.I3.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>) depth within the current image, thereby preserving relative geometric structure (Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV-C Input Normalization ‣ IV Depth Foundation Model ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>-b):</p>
<table id="S4.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{1}=\frac{\log_{p}(D)-\log_{p}(D_{\min})}{\log_{p}(D_{\max})-\log_{p}(D_{\min})}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>min</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{1}=\frac{\log_{p}(D)-\log_{p}(D_{\min})}{\log_{p}(D_{\max})-\log_{p}(D_{\min})}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Mid-Range Norm:
This channel emphasizes the depth regime most relevant for manipulation and indoor interaction (Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV-C Input Normalization ‣ IV Depth Foundation Model ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>-d):</p>
<table id="S4.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{2}=\frac{\log_{p}(D)}{\log_{p}(10)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>10</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{2}=\frac{\log_{p}(D)}{\log_{p}(10)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S4.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Far-Range Norm:
This channel emphasizes the depth regime most relevant for long-range navigation and outdoor scenes (Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV-C Input Normalization ‣ IV Depth Foundation Model ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>-f):</p>
<table id="S4.Ex4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{3}=\frac{\log_{p}(D)}{\log_{p}(100)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>100</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{3}=\frac{\log_{p}(D)}{\log_{p}(100)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, 2) and 3) preserve metric depth at different scales while 1) provides relative depth, allowing for attending to finer details in close range, such as those required for manipulation.
The three channels are stacked to form the final depth input representation:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{\text{in}}=[C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>X</mi><mtext>in</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{\text{in}}=[C_{1},C_{2},C_{3}].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we apply a global mean and standard deviation normalization, computed once across the entire pretraining dataset. As visualized in Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV-C Input Normalization ‣ IV Depth Foundation Model ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, our representation preserves global metric depth, maintains fine-grained near-field structure, and provides stable gradients, yielding a robust and scalable depth representation for self-supervised pretraining.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.18923v1/4_2_input_norm_turbo.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/236;" width="476" height="236" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 3: </span>Visualization of different depth input normalization methods. Log normalization effectively captures the overall depth range while preserving fine-grained structure in near-field regions (b, d, f). In contrast, standard metric normalization yields weaker contrast and poorly separated gradients (c, e). In our representation, we stack columns (b), (d), and (f) to form a 3-channel normalized depth input, which preserves metric depth while maintaining robustness across diverse domains.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS4.4" class="ltx_text">IV-D</span> </span><span id="S4.SS4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Implementation Details</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train our DeFM using the Fully-Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) implementation of DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> and a ViT-L/14 backbone. We prepare two global crops at <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="224^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>224</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">224^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> resolution and eight local crops at <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="98^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>98</mn><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. As in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, we use separate MLP projection heads for DINO and iBOT losses. Training was conducted for <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="625k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>625</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">625k</annotation></semantics></math> iterations on 96 NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper GPUs using a distributed batch size of 3,072. We use AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.5\times 10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5\times 10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math> and a cosine weight decay schedule (<math id="S4.SS4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.04\text{\,}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.04</mn><mtext> </mtext><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.04\text{\,}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.2\text{\,}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.2</mn><mtext> </mtext><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.2\text{\,}</annotation></semantics></math>). We apply a <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100k</annotation></semantics></math> iteration learning rate warmup and update the teacher network’s momentum using a cosine schedule (0.994 to 1.0). All training is performed in float16 precision. Due to computational constraints, we adopt DINOv2 hyperparameters without tuning; for additional details, we refer the reader to the DINOv2 implementation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS5.4" class="ltx_text">IV-E</span> </span><span id="S4.SS5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Distillations</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Knowledge distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib102" title="" class="ltx_ref">102</a>]</cite> aims to transfer the knowledge of a large teacher model into a smaller, more efficient student model by minimizing the distance between their outputs. Since our self-supervised objective is fundamentally a distillation process from the teacher network to the student, we leverage the same training loop with specific modifications to the student network architectures. We use DeFM-L/14 as a frozen teacher for all distillation runs and maintain a separate EMA of the student’s weights, which serves as the final distilled model.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS5.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">IV-E</span>1 </span>Motivation and Target Architectures</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For many downstream RL tasks, the ability to use large batch sizes is critical for stable policy optimization, such as in PPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib103" title="" class="ltx_ref">103</a>]</cite>. Therefore, there is a need for smaller, efficient encoders to minimize memory footprint <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> and faster training times. We thus distill DeFM’s representations into a ViT-S and three lightweight CNN families, namely, ResNets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, RegNets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, and EfficientNets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, ranging in size from <math id="S4.SS5.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S4.SS5.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> parameters.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS5.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">IV-E</span>2 </span>Architectural Adaptation via BiFPN</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Distilling global and dense spatial features from a ViT teacher into a standard CNN student is non-trivial, as typical CNN last-layer global pooling discards the spatial information needed for dense prediction tasks. To ensure the CNN students retain the necessary dense spatial features, we integrate a  <a href="#id21"><span href="#id21" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">BiFPN</span></a> (<a href="#id21"><abbr href="#id21" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">BiFPN</abbr></a>) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib104" title="" class="ltx_ref">104</a>]</cite> on top of our CNN encoders. The <a href="#id21"><abbr href="#id21" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">BiFPN</abbr></a> performs bi-directional fusion of feature maps extracted from the CNN backbone at three distinct resolutions (<math id="S4.SS5.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F/\{8,16,32\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>16</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F/\{8,16,32\}</annotation></semantics></math>). The BiFPN then outputs enhanced, dense spatial features at the same resolutions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S4.SS5.SSS3.4" class="ltx_text">IV-E</span>3 </span>Distillation Strategy and Hyperparameters</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We utilize the same crop strategy as the original pretraining. However, we adjust the input size to align the student and teacher feature maps: we pass global crops of size <math id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256\times 256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>256</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256\times 256</annotation></semantics></math> to the CNN students. This ensures the output spatial feature map from the BiFPN at the <math id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{\prime}/16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>/</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{\prime}/16</annotation></semantics></math> resolution (i.e., <math id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math>) aligns with the spatial tokens of the ViT-L/14 teacher (<math id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="224/14\approx 16\times 16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>224</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>14</mn></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">224/14\approx 16\times 16</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I4" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the DINO losses (<math id="S4.I4.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>DINO</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{DINO}}</annotation></semantics></math>), we match the global pooled feature map of the CNN encoder against the <math id="S4.I4.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathtt{cls}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝚌𝚕𝚜</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathtt{cls}</annotation></semantics></math> token of the frozen ViT teacher.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I4.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the iBOT loss (<math id="S4.I4.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>iBOT</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{iBOT}}</annotation></semantics></math>), we remove the masking and match the dense spatial output of the <a href="#id21"><abbr href="#id21" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">BiFPN</abbr></a> at <math id="S4.I4.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F^{\prime}/16" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>F</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>/</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F^{\prime}/16</annotation></semantics></math> resolution with the spatial patch tokens of the ViT teacher for both global crops.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As before, separate MLP projection heads are used for both the DINO and iBOT losses. We use a multi-student distillation approach for computational efficiency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. Distillation was run for <math id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="200k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>200</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">200k</annotation></semantics></math> iterations on <math id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math> NVIDIA GH200s with a batch size of <math id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2,048" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2,048</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2,048</annotation></semantics></math> and a learning rate of <math id="S4.SS5.SSS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\times 10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\times 10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math> for each student.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.18923v1/4_3_dino_distillation_nord_v2.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/183;" width="429" height="183" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 4: </span>Overview of distilling the DeFM-L/14 teacher into CNN backbones. A BiFPN module is added on top of the CNN encoder to produce dense spatial features, which are supervised using the teacher’s spatial tokens. The teacher’s class token provides global supervision to the CNN’s pooled feature representation.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span><span id="S5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Experiments</span></h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we aim to evaluate the quality and generalizability of the representations learned by DeFM. For a model to be considered truly foundational, its learned features must successfully transfer across different tasks, domains, and sensors. We first provide a qualitative assessment by performing  <a href="#id22"><span href="#id22" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">PCA</span></a> (<a href="#id22"><abbr href="#id22" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">PCA</abbr></a>) on the extracted features (Sec. <a href="#S5.SS1" title="V-A Foundational Depth Image Understanding ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-A</span></a>) to visualize the emergent feature structure. We then quantitatively assess our frozen encoder’s transfer capability across diverse benchmarks. This includes evaluation via linear probing for classification (Sec. <a href="#S5.SS2" title="V-B Classification ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-B</span></a>) and evaluation on the dense prediction task of semantic segmentation (Sec. <a href="#S5.SS3" title="V-C Semantic Segmentation ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-C</span></a>). Lastly, as our focus is on robotic applications, we compare the inference times of all our DeFM and distilled models in Sec. <a href="#S5.SS4" title="V-D Inference Times ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-D</span></a>. We discuss in detail the performance of DeFM for various robotics tasks in a separate dedicated Section (Sec. <a href="#S6" title="VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS1.4" class="ltx_text">V-A</span> </span><span id="S5.SS1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Foundational Depth Image Understanding</span></h3>

<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.18923v1/5_1_cups_pca.png" id="S5.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/474;" width="476" height="474" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 5: </span>PCA visualization of the patch features obtained from the DeFM-L/14 encoder when processing depth images of various cups captured by different sensors. The first three PCA components are mapped to the RGB color channels for visualization. Notice the feature consistency of the cup handle (visualized in yellow) across all images, demonstrating that DeFM learns a useful prior for a robotic grasping task. The background is removed by thresholding the first PCA component.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While depth images provide very strong geometric priors, we argue that meaningful semantic features can also be obtained from them despite the absence of texture and color. To demonstrate this, we perform PCA on features extracted by our DeFM-L/14 encoder.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We collect depth images of various cups using four different depth sensors, namely, Realsense L515 (solid state LiDAR depth camera), Realsense D435i (stereo infrared), ZED 2i (with neural Light depth) and ZED X (with neural Plus depth). We then fit a PCA on the extracted patch features and visualize the first three components, mapping them to RGB channels (Fig. <a href="#S5.F5" title="Fig. 5 ‣ V-A Foundational Depth Image Understanding ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). We observe a strong, consistent correlation between the features and the functional parts of the cup across all sensors. For example, the cup handle is consistently clustered and visualized in yellow, while the cup rim is associated with magenta. The consistency of these semantic features across diverse sensor modalities has significant implications for robotics, serving as a robust prior on where to grasp for downstream policy learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In Fig. <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>-V, the model successfully differentiates and highlights the handles across various types of drawers and cabinets. Overall, these qualitative experiments demonstrate the capability of DeFM to learn generalized, meaningful semantic features robustly across various object classes and depth sensor types.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS2.4" class="ltx_text">V-B</span> </span><span id="S5.SS2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Classification</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The classification task evaluates the quality of the learned visual representations by testing their ability to distinguish between different object categories. Due to the unavailability of a standard classification benchmark for depth images, we create an ImageNet-Depth-1K benchmark consisting of RGB converted depth images estimated from an MDE network <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib85" title="" class="ltx_ref">85</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Linear probing is the standard evaluation protocol for <a href="#id20"><abbr href="#id20" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">VFM</abbr></a>s. In this setup, the pretrained encoder is kept frozen, and only a lightweight linear classifier is trained on labeled data. Strong linear-probe performance indicates that the encoder has learned a feature space where classes are linearly separable, reflecting strong generalization without task-specific fine-tuning. We additionally include top-1 and top-5 KNN accuracy, which evaluates how well the frozen embeddings cluster by retrieving labels from their nearest neighbors in feature space. This training-free evaluation provides a complementary and typically lower-bound estimate of representation quality relative to linear probing.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">TABLE II: </span>Classification evaluations on ImageNet-1k-Depth.</figcaption>

<table id="S5.T2.1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

<th id="S5.T2.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_tt" style="padding:1pt 5.0pt;">Feature</th>
<th id="S5.T2.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:1pt 5.0pt;">Top-1 KNN (↑)</th>

<th id="S5.T2.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_tt" style="padding:1pt 5.0pt;">Linear (↑)</th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S5.T2.1.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S5.T2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding:1pt 5.0pt;">ViT-L/14</th>
<th id="S5.T2.1.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding:1pt 5.0pt;">DINOv2</th>

<section id="S5.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S5.SS2.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">V-B</span>1 </span>Baselines</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare the performance of our models against state-of-the-art <a href="#id20"><abbr href="#id20" title="DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_glossaryref ltx_missing">VFM</abbr></a>s from the RGB domain (inferring on depth images) that represent different pretraining paradigms:</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ViT-L comparison: We compare our largest model, DeFM-L/14, against the self-distilled VFMs: DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> and the more recent DINOv3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. We also include C-RADIOv3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite>, an agglomerative model that distills features from multiple VFMs into a single encoder.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ViT-S comparison: For the smaller, resource-efficient model, DeFM-S/14, we compare against the corresponding size variants of DINOv2 and DINOv3. Since C-RADIOv3 is not available in this small size, we instead use Theia-S <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, which is another agglomerative model specifically distilled for robotics tasks.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For all RGB-pretrained baselines, we perform a min-max normalization to the depth image, stack it into three channels, and finally normalize using the standard ImageNet mean and standard deviation before processing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S5.SS2.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">V-B</span>2 </span>Results</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The quantitative results (Tab. <a href="#S5.T2" title="TABLE II ‣ V-B Classification ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a>) demonstrate the superior feature quality of our DeFM encoder:</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S5.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ViT-L performance: DeFM-L/14 achieves the highest score on both the Top-5 KNN (84.79%) and linear probing (71.72%) metrics, while remaining highly competitive with the DINOv3 model on the Top-1 KNN metric.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ViT-S performance: DeFM-S/14 outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in its size category by up to <math id="S5.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> across all three metrics. This large performance gap highlights the limitations of existing smaller distilled RGB models when applied to depth and strongly reinforces the need for smaller-sized DeFM variants for efficient, high-performance robotic deployments.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Surprisingly, employing depth information alone yields a 71.7% accuracy on a 1000-class object classification task. While this performance is lower than the current state-of-the-art models for RGB input, which achieve around <math id="S5.SS2.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="87.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>87.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">87.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> accuracy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, it clearly demonstrates the intrinsic power of depth data. The result is particularly impressive, given that the classification task includes challenges such as differentiating between various snake species or fine-grained variations in furniture, tasks that typically require human experts to rely on color and texture cues.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S5.SS2.SSS3.4" class="ltx_text">V-B</span>3 </span>Performance of CNNs</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate all of our distilled CNN variants of DeFM to understand the tradeoff between compute time and feature quality, as these smaller models are essential for efficient robotics deployment. The results are summarized in Tab. <a href="#S5.T3" title="TABLE III ‣ V-B Classification ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III</span></a>. As expected, we observe a general drop in performance correlating with decreasing model size.
However, we note a surprisingly strong result: some of the very small CNN models, such as RegNetY-400MF (4.1 M), outperform the ViT-S RGB baselines (22.1 M) (Tab. <a href="#S5.T2" title="TABLE II ‣ V-B Classification ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a>) across all three metrics.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS3.4" class="ltx_text">V-C</span> </span><span id="S5.SS3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Semantic Segmentation</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Semantic segmentation is a critical evaluation task for VFMs, as it directly assesses the quality of dense spatial features, which are essential for most robotic tasks, such as grasp localization, obstacle avoidance, and scene understanding. To assess whether the frozen DeFM encoder provides meaningful per-pixel representations, we perform linear-probe segmentation. Following the standard protocol, we train a linear layer to predict the class logits from the patch tokens. The output is then upsampled to the full resolution using bilinear interpolation to obtain the final segmentation map. We use the same baselines that were introduced earlier for classification in Sec. <a href="#S5.SS2.SSS1" title="V-B1 Baselines ‣ V-B Classification ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V-B1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S5.SS3.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">V-C</span>1 </span>Datasets</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An ideal foundation model must demonstrate robust generalization across diverse domains and sensor types. Accordingly, we select 5 diverse depth datasets for evaluating semantic segmentation, ensuring coverage across varied environments and acquisition modalities.
These benchmarks range from indoor room settings and fine-grained tabletop manipulation scenarios to large-scale outdoor navigation environments. The datasets have been summarized in Tab. <a href="#S5.T4" title="TABLE IV ‣ V-C1 Datasets ‣ V-C Semantic Segmentation ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a>.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S5.SS3.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">V-C</span>2 </span>Results</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The quantitative results in terms of mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) are summarized in Tab. <a href="#S5.T5" title="TABLE V ‣ V-C2 Results ‣ V-C Semantic Segmentation ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V</span></a>. Overall, DeFM models demonstrate robust generalization across different domains and surpass existing baselines in the majority of benchmarks. For the ViT-L architecture, DeFM-L/14 achieves the highest mIoU scores across four out of five datasets, while the performance improvement is particularly pronounced for the ViT-S architecture. Consistent with our classification findings, the generalization gap is significant, with DeFM-S/14 achieving mIoU scores up to <math id="S5.SS3.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">30\%</annotation></semantics></math> higher than the corresponding baselines in several benchmarks. We illustrate the improvement qualitatively by comparing the segmentation output of DINOv3-S/16 with our DeFM-S/14 in Fig. <a href="#S5.F6" title="Fig. 6 ‣ V-C2 Results ‣ V-C Semantic Segmentation ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.
Finally, our smaller distilled ResNet models consistently outperform the similar-sized baseline models on almost all datasets, providing strong geometric and semantic features for resource-constrained robotic deployments.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S5.SS4.4" class="ltx_text">V-D</span> </span><span id="S5.SS4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Inference Times</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To facilitate informed hardware planning, we report comprehensive metrics for all models in the DeFM family in Tab. <a href="#S5.T6" title="TABLE VI ‣ V-D Inference Times ‣ V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI</span></a>. This evaluation provides a crucial guideline for understanding the tradeoff between training times, memory consumption, and performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We report the inference latency and VRAM consumption on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (using a large batch size, <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{BS}=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>BS</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{BS}=128</annotation></semantics></math>), which is a typical GPU used to train downstream RL policies. Furthermore, we report the inference time for a single image (<math id="S5.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{BS}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>BS</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{BS}=1</annotation></semantics></math>) on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, a representative platform for real-world robotic deployments. We use images of size <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="224\times 224" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>224</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>224</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">224\times 224</annotation></semantics></math> for all reported numbers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our results highlight that inference speed on the Orin edge hardware is highly dependent on the model’s architecture itself, rather than solely on parameter count: RegNetY models, which often incorporate features like Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) layers, and EfficientNet models, which rely on depth-wise separable convolutions, show unexpectedly high latency on the Orin platform as these operations are not always fully optimized in standard PyTorch execution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">It is important to note that all reported timings are measured using the standard PyTorch framework, and no model runtime optimizations (e.g., TensorRT/ONNX conversion) were performed. Utilizing such optimizations is expected to reduce the latency across all models, particularly on the resource-constrained Orin platform.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VI </span><span id="S6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Robotic Experiments</span></h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While our analysis in Sec. <a href="#S5" title="V Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">V</span></a> established the strong generalization of DeFM’s frozen features on standard perception tasks (classification and segmentation), the main motivation of this work is to provide representations that are directly usable for RL, ideally without any task-specific fine-tuning. Solving complex, embodied control tasks requires features that are not just semantically meaningful but are geometrically grounded and action-relevant.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the quality of our DeFM representations on downstream tasks, we select four distinct and challenging RL tasks across navigation, manipulation, and locomotion. Specifically, our evaluation includes:</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S6.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Habitat Point-Goal Nav</span> (Sec. <a href="#S6.SS1" title="VI-A Navigation: Habitat Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI-A</span></a>): A standard benchmark in the Habitat simulator <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite> where an agent must navigate to a target 3D goal point in various indoor scenes using a discrete set of actions.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav</span> (Sec. <a href="#S6.SS2" title="VI-B Navigation: Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI-B</span></a>): Utilizing the Unitree B2W wheeled-legged robot, this long-range task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> tests navigation policies that must handle the robot’s kinematics and physical footprint, prioritizing accurate geometric obstacle avoidance.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dexterous Grasping</span> (Sec. <a href="#S6.SS3" title="VI-C Manipulation: Dexterous Grasping ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI-C</span></a>): Using a KUKA-Allegro arm-hand setup, the agent is tasked with grasping a diverse range of objects <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Quadrupedal Ladder Climbing</span> (Sec. <a href="#S6.SS4" title="VI-D Locomotion: Quadruped Ladder Climbing ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI-D</span></a>): This challenging locomotion task requires the ANYbotics ANYmal quadruped to robustly climb ladders of varying sizes and angles <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">107</a>]</cite>. The policy relies on proprioception and features derived from four depth cameras to ensure stable footholds and gait synchronization.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In the subsequent subsections, we discuss in detail the setup, baselines, and evaluations for each of the tasks. Unless otherwise stated, we always use a frozen DeFM encoder and only train the downstream policy network.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS1.4" class="ltx_text">VI-A</span> </span><span id="S6.SS1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Navigation: Habitat Point-Goal Nav</span></h3>

<section id="S6.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS1.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">VI-A</span>1 </span>Setup and Baselines</h4>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This task uses the Habitat Point-Goal Navigation benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite>, where the agent must navigate to a target goal point in various multi-room multi-floor environments. The policy is optimized using Decentralized Distributed Proximal Policy Optimization (DD-PPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>. The policy architecture utilizes a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) network to process features extracted from the visual encoder.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Training was conducted on the Gibson train set for <math id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="75\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>75</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">75\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> steps using <math id="S6.SS1.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>32</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">32</annotation></semantics></math> environments distributed across 4 GPUs. We compare the performance of our frozen DeFM-S/14 and DeFM-ResNet-50 against several baselines in the competitive size category:</p>
<ul id="S6.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S6.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Scratch Baseline: ResNet-50 trained entirely from scratch, as commonly done in prior literature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Frozen VFMs: ViT-S variants of DINOv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, <span id="S6.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">DINOv3</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, and Theia <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS1.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">VI-A</span>2 </span>Results</h4>

<figure id="S6.T7" class="ltx_table">

<th id="S6.T7.1.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;">DeFM</th>

<td id="S6.T7.1.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-top:1pt;padding-bottom:1pt;">0.7509</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The evaluation results are measured by Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) and are summarized in Tab. <a href="#S6.T7" title="TABLE VII ‣ VI-A2 Results ‣ VI-A Navigation: Habitat Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VII</span></a>. We train each model three times and report the average performance. The frozen DeFM models outperform all other frozen foundation model baselines across both evaluation sets (Gibson validation and MatterPort3D validation). We note that DINOv3 also shows remarkable performance on depth data, however, both of our DeFM models outperform it. On the other hand, Theia, which was specifically distilled for robotics tasks, and DINOv2 do not perform that well on depth data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our best distilled model, DeFM-ResNet-50, achieves competitive performance compared to the ResNet-50 trained entirely from scratch, demonstrating the value of pretraining in avoiding the cost and complexity associated with training task-specific encoders. These results highlight that DeFM’s frozen features are directly usable and highly effective for depth-based navigation policies.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS2.4" class="ltx_text">VI-B</span> </span><span id="S6.SS2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Navigation: Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav</span></h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Having demonstrated that DeFM features are useful for navigation, we next test their transferability in a more realistic and challenging scenario. For this, we select the point goal navigation task introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> and utilize the Unitree B2W wheeled legged robot. In this task, the policy must perform long-range navigation over diverse terrains and complex environments while actively avoiding obstacles using a single front-facing depth camera as input.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS2.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">VI-B</span>1 </span>Setup and Baselines</h4>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For encoding the depth images, the authors pretrain a Variational Auto Encoder (VAE) on <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite> using reconstruction loss, which is kept frozen during the RL policy training. A compact RegNetX-400MF encoder, along with a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN), is used to encode the depth images. The dense output of the FPN is then used to perform cross attention with the proprioceptive data and processed by a Spatially-enhanced Recurrent Unit (SRU) block and a few MLP layers to generate the final velocity commands, which are then tracked by a low-level locomotion policy. To perform a fair comparison with this baseline, we distill our DeFM ViT-L/14 into the same network architecture on the full DeFM depth dataset. Additionally, we also distill DinoV3-L features on the DeFM dataset into the same network as an additional baseline. For training the downstream RL policy, we adopt the exact same hyperparameters specified in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> and train on a single <span id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">RTX 4090</span> GPU. Downsampled depth images of size <math id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 40</annotation></semantics></math> are used as an input to the network.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the performance using the Success Rate (SR) metric, where a run is considered successful if the agent manages to reach the goal-point within <math id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="120" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>120</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">120</annotation></semantics></math> seconds. Apart from evaluating in the training environment, we set up three realistic, geometrically complex TartanGround <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib89" title="" class="ltx_ref">89</a>]</cite> meshes in Gazebo simulation for realistic out-of-distribution evaluation (Fig. <a href="#S6.F7" title="Fig. 7 ‣ VI-B2 Results ‣ VI-B Navigation: Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>). These consist of Industrial Hangar (b), Abandoned Cable (c), and the Modern City Downtown (d) environments. These environments depict realistic scenarios for deployments and are quite different from the training environment (a), which primarily consists of mazes, pits, and staircases. We randomly sample <math id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>100</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100</annotation></semantics></math> navigable start-end goal pairs in each of the environments within a range of <math id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\text{\,}\mathrm{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\text{\,}\mathrm{m}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="80\text{\,}\mathrm{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>80</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">80\text{\,}\mathrm{m}</annotation></semantics></math>. We evaluate each policy <math id="S6.SS2.SSS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> times and report the average SR. We discuss the results obtained in the simulation in the following subsection, after which we proceed to perform real-world experiments in Sec. <a href="#S6.SS2.SSS3" title="VI-B3 Real World Deployments ‣ VI-B Navigation: Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI-B3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS2.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">VI-B</span>2 </span>Results</h4>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results have been summarized in Tab. <a href="#S6.T8" title="TABLE VIII ‣ VI-B2 Results ‣ VI-B Navigation: Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VIII</span></a>. While the VAE baseline achieves similar performance to our DeFM in the training, we achieve improved performance during testing, particularly in the Abandoned Cable and Modern City Downtown environments. Upon a closer examination of the individual failure cases, we notice that, in general, the policy utilizing our DeFM model performs better at avoiding thin and out-of-distribution (OOD) obstacles, such as fences, traffic signs, lamp posts, etc. We hypothesize that our DeFM model is able to better recognize the OOD obstacles and intrinsically assign higher costs to those obstacles, which the VAE might fail to do.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In Fig. <a href="#S6.F8" title="Fig. 8 ‣ VI-B2 Results ‣ VI-B Navigation: Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, we quantitatively analyse the failure cases by breaking them down in terms of collision and timeouts. We can consider the collision failures as a perception failure arising primarily due to the encoder, while the timeout usually occurs when the navigation policy is stuck in a local minima. We notice that DeFM consistently has lower collision failures than the other two baselines, highlighting the better geometric and semantic understanding of the environment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we notice that DINOv3 performs the worst of all compared encoders. One reason we hypothesize for this underperformance is the model’s inability to retain the metric depth understanding. Unlike our DeFM, where the input normalization explicitly attempts to preserve and learn across vast metric scales, DINOv3 treats depth simply as another intensity channel. This result further demonstrates the importance of preserving metric depth for successful transfer to embodiment-aware robotic tasks.</p>
</div>
