<section id="S6.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS2.SSS3.4" class="ltx_text">VI-B</span>3 </span>Real World Deployments</h4>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To demonstrate successful sim-to-real transfer, we test our DeFM encoder-based policy in four diverse, challenging real-world environments, including a confined obstacle-rich indoor setting, an outdoor urban environment, an unstructured park environment, and a high-clutter construction site (Fig. <a href="#S6.F9" title="Fig. 9 ‣ VI-B3 Real World Deployments ‣ VI-B Navigation: Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>). We test multiple start-goal endpoints ranging from <math id="S6.SS2.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S6.SS2.SSS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}</annotation></semantics></math> and observe that our policy generalizes effectively to these environments, handling diverse obstacles such as pedestrians, scooters, barriers, furniture, etc., as well as navigating uneven terrains. We visualize one of the deployments from the park environment in Fig. <a href="#S6.F10" title="Fig. 10 ‣ VI-B3 Real World Deployments ‣ VI-B Navigation: Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> and refer to the supplementary video for more deployments.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F9" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.18923v1/6_3_sru_real.png" id="S6.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/284;" width="476" height="284" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 9: </span>Real world deployments using a Unitree B2W robot in diverse environments- (A) Indoor, (B) Urban, (C) Park, (D) Construction Site.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S6.F10" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.18923v1/6_3_uni_nav.png" id="S6.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/354;" width="476" height="354" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 10: </span>Real world deployment in a park environment with a goal point at around <math id="S6.F10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="90\text{\,}\mathrm{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>90</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">90\text{\,}\mathrm{m}</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS2.SSS4.4" class="ltx_text">VI-B</span>4 </span>Discussions and Limitations</h4>

<div id="S6.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While the authors in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> also demonstrate sim-to-real transfer in diverse environments, our result is particularly impressive since, unlike the VAE, which needs to be pretrained with a specific noise model, depth clippings (<math id="S6.SS2.SSS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{m}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S6.SS2.SSS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\text{\,}\mathrm{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\text{\,}\mathrm{m}</annotation></semantics></math>), and additional hand-engineering, our DeFM encoder works out of the box without any task-specific heuristics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS2.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, one of the failure cases that we observe is that the policy occasionally struggles with very small or thin obstacles such as wires, poles, or mesh structures (even in simulation). We attribute this primarily to the low spatial resolution of the depth input (<math id="S6.SS2.SSS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64\times 40" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>64</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64\times 40</annotation></semantics></math>) used during the policy training, a design choice made by the authors in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> to ease the sim-to-real transfer and computational constraints. Despite the low resolution, the policy reliably handles complex clutter, indicating that DeFM already provides strong features even under heavy compression. We expect that scaling simulation diversity and input resolution will allow the policy to realize the full potential of the DeFM features, improving sensitivity to fine-grained geometry and mitigating these remaining failure cases.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS3.4" class="ltx_text">VI-C</span> </span><span id="S6.SS3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Manipulation: Dexterous Grasping</span></h3>

<section id="S6.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS3.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">VI-C</span>1 </span>Setup and Baselines</h4>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider the dexterous arm-hand grasping from DexTRAH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite> (Fig. <a href="#S6.F11" title="Fig. 11 ‣ VI-C1 Setup and Baselines ‣ VI-C Manipulation: Dexterous Grasping ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>). Following the prior work, the teacher is trained using state-based information, comprising of privileged information such as the object state and its one-hot encoding. The teacher policy is distilled into a student policy, which receives depth images instead of stereo RGB images. The depth images are encoded using DeFM and concatenated with the proprioceptive information before feeding it to an LSTM and MLP architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our DeFM-pretrained ResNet-18 against two representative baselines: a standard ResNet-18 pretrained on RGB ImageNet, and a distilled ResNet-18 trained to match the embeddings of the DINOv3 ViT-L/16 teacher on our DeFM dataset.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We compare two training setups: frozen pretrained networks and end-to-end finetuning during teacher-student policy distillation. We also compare these with an encoder trained from scratch during the student distillation process. The training hyperparameters are kept the same as the prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">79</a>]</cite>. The student policies are trained using Isaac Lab <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">81</a>]</cite> using distributed training on eight NVIDIA L40S GPUs, each running 256 parallel environments. The environment provides depth observations augmented with speckle noise, Gaussian noise, pixel dropout, and stick noise <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F11" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3"><img src="2601.18923v1/figures/dextrah/sim-3/08_t0035.png" id="S6.F11.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:155/289;" width="155" height="289" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3"><img src="2601.18923v1/figures/dextrah/sim-3/08_t0090.png" id="S6.F11.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:155/289;" width="155" height="289" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3"><img src="2601.18923v1/figures/dextrah/sim-3/08_t0150.png" id="S6.F11.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:155/289;" width="155" height="289" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3"><img src="2601.18923v1/figures/dextrah/depth-3/08_t0035.png" id="S6.F11.g4" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:155/207;" width="155" height="207" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3"><img src="2601.18923v1/figures/dextrah/depth-3/08_t0090.png" id="S6.F11.g5" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:155/207;" width="155" height="207" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3"><img src="2601.18923v1/figures/dextrah/depth-3/08_t0150.png" id="S6.F11.g6" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:155/207;" width="155" height="207" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 11: </span>Rollout of DeFM model for dexterous grasping using the Kuka-Allegro setup. Bottom: The simulated noisy depth images used during training.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S6.F12" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.18923v1/dextrah_depth_noise.png" id="S6.F12.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/171;" width="476" height="171" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 12: </span>Depth images input to the dexterous grasping policy. During training, images are augmented with speckles, dropout, and stick noise. For evaluations, we also consider depth images augmented with the Kinect noise model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib108" title="" class="ltx_ref">108</a>]</cite>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS3.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">VI-C</span>2 </span>Results</h4>

<div id="S6.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the trained policies in two scenarios: (i) the same noise model as during training, and (ii) using the Kinect noise model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib108" title="" class="ltx_ref">108</a>]</cite>, which adds edge and distance noise to the depth image, to evaluate robustness to realistic sensor noise. A representative scenario with the different noise models is shown in Fig. <a href="#S6.F12" title="Fig. 12 ‣ VI-C1 Setup and Baselines ‣ VI-C Manipulation: Dexterous Grasping ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>. Tab. <a href="#S6.T9" title="TABLE IX ‣ VI-C2 Results ‣ VI-C Manipulation: Dexterous Grasping ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IX</span></a> reports the average success rate (normalized to the teacher policy) across 2,000 episodes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The fine-tuned DeFM model achieves the highest performance across both scenarios, and fine-tuning improves results for all models. Notably, the frozen DeFM encoder outperforms both the scratch-trained encoder and fine-tuned ImageNet encoder, while achieving competitive performance relative to the fine-tuned DINOv3 baseline. This highlights the strong geometric and semantic priors learnt by DeFM.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Under the alternative Kinect noise model, frozen models experience a significant performance drop, likely because the MLP on top of frozen features overfits to the training depth images. Among the frozen models, DeFM provides more consistent features, resulting in a smaller decline. Fine-tuned DeFM is the least affected by changes in the noise model, demonstrating both the adaptability and stability of its task-specific features.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS3.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Lastly, we present qualitative results by performing PCA on real-world depth images captured with a ZED camera from the DROID dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib97" title="" class="ltx_ref">97</a>]</cite>. In the complex, cluttered kitchen scenes, the DeFM feature space exhibits a clear structure: PCA embeddings cluster different scene components such as the countertop, background surfaces, robot arm, and manipulable objects (Fig. <a href="#S6.F13" title="Fig. 13 ‣ VI-C2 Results ‣ VI-C Manipulation: Dexterous Grasping ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T9" class="ltx_table">

<section id="S6.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S6.SS4.4" class="ltx_text">VI-D</span> </span><span id="S6.SS4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Locomotion: Quadruped Ladder Climbing</span></h3>

<section id="S6.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS4.SSS1.4" class="ltx_text">VI-D</span>1 </span>Setup and Baselines</h4>

<div id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the performance of DeFM on a locomotion task, we consider perceptive quadrupedal ladder climbing (Fig. <a href="#S6.F14" title="Fig. 14 ‣ VI-D1 Setup and Baselines ‣ VI-D Locomotion: Quadruped Ladder Climbing ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>) by adapting techniques from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib107" title="" class="ltx_ref">107</a>]</cite>. The controller is trained using a teacher–student setup where the teacher is trained with privileged information that the perceptive student learns to mimic. The student network consists of a CNN encoder, which produces the depth embeddings, which are concatenated with the proprioceptive measurements and processed by an RNN network to produce the actions. For the baseline, we follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite> and train the CNN encoder from scratch, which we compare with our frozen RegNetX-400MF DeFM encoder, which was introduced in Sec. <a href="#S6.SS2" title="VI-B Navigation: Embodiment Aware Point-Goal Nav ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">VI-B</span></a>. The policy is trained in IsaacGym <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib109" title="" class="ltx_ref">109</a>]</cite> using 1,024 parallel environments, collecting 120 steps per batch over 10,000 training epochs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F14" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.18923v1/6_8_ladder_climbing.png" id="S6.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/226;" width="476" height="226" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 14: </span>ANYmal climbing a ladder, shown together with noisy depth image (top row) from onboard camera.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection"><span id="S6.SS4.SSS2.4" class="ltx_text">VI-D</span>2 </span>Results</h4>

<div id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the trained polices across a setup consisting of varying ladder rung radii (15 mm to 45 mm with 5 mm increments) and ladder angles (70° - 90° with 5°  intervals) while applying random disturbances. Each combination is tested for 750 episodes with 1024 environments. We use the Success Rate (SR) metric for comparison, where the episode is considered a success if the robot manages to climb the ladder within 15 seconds. Our DeFM model (90.14%) matches the performance of the CNN baseline trained from scratch (90.45%) while requiring substantially less compute. This demonstrates that our encoder can be transferred to challenging locomotion tasks, without any task-specific fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS4.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Since our model was trained to handle sensor noise and varying depth data, we hypothesize an even stronger generalization for sim-to-real transfer compared to the CNN baseline.
Preliminarily, we present some qualitative results by performing PCA on depth images collected during a ladder-climbing deployment. As seen in Fig. <a href="#S6.F15" title="Fig. 15 ‣ VI-D2 Results ‣ VI-D Locomotion: Quadruped Ladder Climbing ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>, our DeFM is able to consistently assign similar features to the ladder structure despite the heavy noise inherent in real-world stereo depth cameras.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.F15" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2601.18923v1/6_8_ladder_pca.png" id="S6.F15.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/251;" width="476" height="251" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 15: </span>PCA visualization for real-world images collected during deployment of ANYmal ladder-climbing in the wild.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VII </span><span id="S7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Conclusion and Future Work</span></h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduced DeFM, a family of depth image encoders pretrained using self-supervision on a curated depth dataset of <math id="S7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60\text{\,}\mathrm{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>60</mn><mtext> </mtext><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60\text{\,}\mathrm{M}</annotation></semantics></math> depth images. DeFM learns robust geometric and semantic features that generalize across tasks, environments, and sensors. Our results show that DeFM serves as an effective off-the-shelf depth encoder for a wide range of robot perception and control tasks, including classification, segmentation, navigation, locomotion, and manipulation without any task-specific fine-tuning. Moreover, it enables robust sim-to-real transfer across diverse real-world settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A key outcome of this work is the effectiveness of our distilled variants, which retain most of the representational strength of the large model while offering substantial gains in efficiency. These compact models make it practical to deploy strong depth representations on resource-constrained robotic systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">DeFM has the potential to streamline depth perception across a wide range of robotic systems. A single frozen depth encoder could replace many of the engineering-heavy pipelines still common today, such as reliance on elevation maps for perceptive locomotion or task-specific depth preprocessing stages. Our results show that frozen depth foundation models can enable fast and efficient RL training, pointing toward a future where depth-based representations offer a simple, general, and high-performing alternative to task-specific depth-processing modules.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p4.1" class="ltx_p">While DeFM delivers strong features across domains, we observe occasional artifacts in the learned representations (Figs. <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>-V, <a href="#S6.F15" title="Fig. 15 ‣ VI-D2 Results ‣ VI-D Locomotion: Quadruped Ladder Climbing ‣ VI Robotic Experiments ‣ DeFM: Learning Foundation Representations from Depth for Robotics" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>), a known limitation of ViT architectures. These artifacts can likely be mitigated through architectural refinements such as the use of register tokens <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib110" title="" class="ltx_ref">110</a>]</cite>. Our real-world experiments, though promising, are currently limited in terms of task diversity due to hardware constraints. Expanding to an even broader range of platforms and tasks is an important next step. Another exciting direction is scaling DeFM to depth measurements obtained from solid-state LiDARs and LiDAR range-image representations, extending its applicability beyond standard stereo/IR depth sensors. Finally, following trends demonstrated by DINOv3, increasing dataset diversity, model capacity, and training iterations is likely to yield even more powerful depth foundation models with improved generalization capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>

      all.</p>
